articles.title: A 73-year-old Texas law professor collapsed during class and stopped breathing; a Navy SEAL veteran in his classroom performed three rounds of CPR, and the professor has now returned to teaching after surviving
articles.summary: The classroom can be the place for lessons that go way beyond textbooks, examinations and academic degrees.
articles.body: The classroom can be the place for lessons that go way beyond textbooks, examinations and academic degrees. For 73-year-old Michael Maslanka, a professor of law at the University of North Texas at Dallas (UNT Dallas) College of Law, an average evening class became a life-and-death situation. His own students, not medical professionals, were his first line of rescue when his heart suddenly failed. Their quick action, especially that of a former Navy SEAL, helped give the professor another chance at life, letting him return to the classroom and deliver a powerful message about the importance of learning CPR.The classroom emergency that changed everythingFOX 4 reports Maslanka was in the middle of teaching an evening class on October 8, 2026, when he began experiencing blurred vision and feeling too ill to continue. He told his students he was unable to finish the lesson when he fell to the floor.The professor's pulse was lost, he stopped breathing and things quickly became critical. What followed was a coordinated emergency response, and some students didn’t wait around helplessly.Matthew Melton, 45, a cybersecurity professional and third-year law student, is a former Navy SEAL who was among them. Melton knew he had to act immediately and determined that Maslanka was not breathing and began CPR.Navy SEAL training becomes a life-saving skillAccording to UNT Dallas, Melton performed three rounds of CPR, alternating between chest compressions and rescue breaths. It was a physically demanding procedure and he remembered hearing Maslanka's ribs break during the compressions. But he knew that right now, the priority was to keep blood flowing and give his professor a chance at survival.Melton was not the only one. Law students Anwar Hannon and Jeff Baza rendered aid, while Daniella Sanchez called 911 and helped coordinate the response. She also clasped the professor's hand and prayed for his recovery.Other students helped direct emergency responders into the building. Their combined efforts ensured that help could reach Maslanka without undue delay.Melton’s ability to react was the result of years of military service. He’d been trained in CPR as a teen, taught others the procedure, and witnessed advanced battlefield medical training during his Navy service. His deployments included Iraq in 2005 and Bahrain in 2001.Doctors administer electric shock twiceEmergency responders eventually took Maslanka to Dallas’ Baylor University Medical Center, where he was treated by doctors who worked to stabilize his condition.The doctors “zapped” his heart twice, CBS News reported. The professor had suffered ventricular tachycardia, a potentially fatal heart rhythm disorder in which the heart’s lower chambers beat too fast, preventing the heart from pumping blood effectively.Maslanka spent two days in intensive care, then was transferred to a regular hospital room. He later recovered enough to leave the hospital and return to teaching.He has repeatedly expressed his gratitude to his students for saving his life, noting that the CPR they performed kept him alive long enough to receive emergency care.A remarkable link between teacher and studentsInterestingly, in a 2014 video for Texas Bar TV on professional excellence, Maslanka used Navy SEALs as an example of discipline and preparation. He urged lawyers to emulate their example of constant training and readiness.More than a decade later, that lesson took an unexpectedly personal turn when a former SEAL student helped save his life.The incident also deepened the emotional connection between Maslanka and his students. A week after the emergency, Sanchez and classmates visited him in hospital, an emotional reunion which showed how much the experience had affected everyone.Professor comes back with a message for everyoneNow back in the classroom, Maslanka wants his experience to mean more than just his own recovery. As reported by UNT Dallas and FOX 4, he is urging people to learn CPR and get certified so that they are able to respond with confidence when someone is experiencing a cardiac emergency.UNT Health physician Jeff Beeson also stressed the need for CPR, noting the students’ actions were a good example of how basic knowledge of saving lives can make a difference.Maslanka is writing an article for Texas Lawyer, "Four Life Hacks That Dying (Twice) Taught Me." The experience has made a common academic lesson a lasting memorial for the professor of human preparedness, compassion and responsibility. His students came to class to learn law, but that nite they showed a skill that was just as important, the ability to defend another person’s life when every second counts.Images Courtesy: UNT DallasYou use AI every day. articles.title: Paranoid or practical? Britain’s ‘Be Ready’ citizen campaign
articles.summary: People in England and Wales are rushing to buy tinned goods and wind-up radios – but what’s it all for?
articles.body:
The British government’s “Be Ready” campaign has caused a rush on tinned goods, bringing back memories of the COVID-19 pandemic when supermarkets ran dangerously low on toilet paper and online vendors were price-gouging on the internet.

In the 10 days since the campaign urging citizens in England and Wales to be ready for a national emergency was launched on October 22, sales of bottled water have risen by 67 percent; tinned and jarred food by 37 percent; and hand sanitiser by 83 percent, according to retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator. Wind-up radios, torches and power banks have also sold out at several retailers.

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, the campaign’s most prominent public face, says the government wants people to be “alert but not alarmed”. So what is Be Ready, why now, and is it really necessary?

Be Ready is a three-year public information campaign being run by the Cabinet Office. Its launch on October 22 marked its first stage.

The government is asking households in England and Wales to make sure they would be able to cope on their own for 72 hours if electricity, water, phone and internet services all fail in the event of a national emergency. The idea is that emergency services can then focus on people who require more urgent assistance.

The campaign’s website features a checklist, starting with bottled water and long-life food that does not need to be kept in a fridge, such as tinned food, dried fruit and nuts.

It also recommends having a torch, spare batteries, a charged power bank and a wind-up or battery-powered radio, along with cash in case card payments go down, a first aid kit, medication, warm clothing and blankets to hand.

The new website covers England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland receive their own advice through Ready Scotland and NI Direct.

More than 500 organisations, including charities, businesses and faith and community groups, have signed up to spread the message.

Official household preparedness guidance has existed since May 2024. What is new is the push to get people to act on it.

Officially, the focus of the campaign is to ensure households can get through “everyday emergencies” such as storms, floods, wildfires and burst water pipes. The campaign follows months of heatwaves, drought and fires across the United Kingdom this summer.

The government also highlights how unprepared Britons say they are. In a Cabinet Office survey this year, only 13 percent said their household was largely or totally prepared for an emergency, while 84 percent wanted more advice from the government.

Independent research points the same way. A 2025 survey of 931 people by Bournemouth University’s Disaster Management Centre, part of its EM-PREPARE project, found that only 52 percent felt they understood the hazards they faced, and 21 percent said they were not aware of the risks at all. The same study found that 81 percent were willing to do more to prepare.

In September, the National Audit Office, the UK’s spending watchdog, warned of threats facing Britain’s food supply chain.

The security backdrop features, too. Ministers have linked the campaign to the risk of cyberattacks and hostile state activity against critical infrastructure. On Remembrance Day, Defence Minister Lord Coaker said the 13 percent figure was exactly why the campaign had been launched.

The UK is also catching up with its neighbours. The European Commission’s Preparedness Union Strategy, adopted in March 2025, recommends that people be able to cope alone for at least 72 hours. Sweden posted 5.2 million copies of its crisis-preparedness brochure to households in November 2024, and Finland, Poland and the Czech Republic run similar campaigns.

Shoppers in England and Wales have acted fast and enthusiastically. Supermarket chain Iceland said sales of tinned products rose 40 percent over the first weekend. Tinned-food producer Princes reported particularly high demand for tuna, meat and vegetables.

Worldpanel found the equivalent of 400,000 extra people a day bought tinned meat immediately after the launch.

Meanwhile, Canned Food UK, part of the Metal Packaging Manufacturers Association, has launched a consumer campaign featuring TV chef and author Theo Michaels, who demonstrates how to use canned food in tasty recipes.

The rush has extended beyond the food aisles. Electronics retailer Maplin said torch sales jumped 284 percent; radios, 92 percent; and power banks, 106 percent, within days. Hardware store group Robert Dyas reported a 160 percent rise in radio sales, and at least seven wind-up radio models sold out across several outlets.

Criticism has focused on tone more than substance. On BBC’s Question Time, an audience member accused Streeting of “scaremongering”, warning that the advice would trigger panic buying. Streeting replied that the campaign was about everyday threats such as wildfires, flooding and frozen pipes.

Opposition figures have largely accepted the principle. Conservative Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat called the advice “a perfectly reasonable thing”.

Analysts and charities are split on who should carry the burden. The British Red Cross, a campaign partner, has backed it, saying simple preparation helps people support friends, family and neighbours.

But more than 180 experts, academics, farmers and community food leaders signed an open letter warning that 29 percent of Britons cannot afford a three-day food reserve. They urged ministers to set up national, regional and community food stores rather than rely on the resilience of individual households.

How ready are British households for an emergency?

On November 2, Parliament’s Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy took evidence on public preparedness. Among the witnesses was Lee Miles, professor of crisis and disaster management at Bournemouth University, who led the EM-PREPARE study of household resilience.

His research found that 75 percent of households had no major measures in place to cope with climate change, and about 69 percent were willing to spend no more than one day improving their preparedness.

Miles told the committee that the challenge was to move from raising awareness to helping people act. “The important thing about the ‘Be Ready’ campaign is turning it into a ‘Being Ready’ campaign,” he said.

Miles also warned that local resilience bodies would need proper funding if they were given more responsibility. “Otherwise, you set them up to fail in various aspects; they will not be able to deliver what they are supposed to,” he told MPs.

Supporters say the advice is modest and overdue. Having three days of supplies is standard across much of Europe, and the 2025 Iberian blackout showed how fast cash machines, card payments and mobile networks can fail.

That was when Spain, Portugal and parts of southwestern France were hit by a widespread power blackout that paralysed public transport, caused large traffic jams, delayed flights, and left residents unable to access cash from ATMs, as utility operators and the authorities scrambled to restore the electric grid.

With only one in eight Britons feeling prepared, they argue, a calm campaign now is better than a panicked one during a crisis. Retail data so far suggests most people have responded calmly.

The Bournemouth research highlights why the messaging could be critical. Households responding to that said they saw accidents at home as the hazard most likely to affect them – cited by 35 percent – while only 5 percent named war and conflict, and 4 percent terrorism.

Miles called for more targeted risk communication to the public, alongside education to help households build their resilience.

articles.title: Battle-tested in Operation Sindoor, now getting an AI upgrade: India's air defence system is set to get smarter
articles.summary: Recent and ongoing conflicts have demonstrated the importance of air defences.
articles.body: Recent and ongoing conflicts have demonstrated the importance of air defences. From the use of air power during Operation Sindoor, when Pakistan's efforts to damage key Indian military capabilities failed miserably, to the conflict in West Asia and Ukraine, where the need for robust air defence has emerged as the most critical factor. When a drone, a cruise missile or a fighter crosses into Indian airspace, the decision about what to do next increasingly takes just seconds. The system that makes this possible is the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS), and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) says it has now completed development of the critical core technologies for its next-generation upgrade, which aims to make the Indian Air Force's air-defence network AI-native.What IACCS isIACCS is an automated command and control network for air defence, run by the Indian Air Force (IAF) and built around BEL's systems. It runs on the Air Force Network (AFNET), the encrypted digital grid launched on September 14, 2010, and brings together data from ground radars, airborne warning aircraft, drones, air traffic control and civil radars, air-defence weapons and command nodes. From these, it builds a single Recognised Air Situation Picture, so commanders at every level can see the same airspace in real time. The IACCs has multiple nodes and sub-nodes across the nation.The upgradeThe new version adds an AI-native decision-support architecture that scores and ranks threats, including drones, cruise missiles and saturation raids, and recommends the best weapon, whether a long-range interceptor such as the S-400 or Project Kusha class, a medium-range system like Akash-NG, or a fighter intercept. It fuses data from radars such as the indigenous Arudhra and Ashwini, Netra airborne warning aircraft, satellite feeds and fighter sensors, and has in-house cybersecurity hardening and standoff launch detection. A human commander stays in the loop. The network now links the IAF with Akashteer and the Navy's Trigun maritime domain-awareness network through the Joint Air Defence Centre, creating a common operational picture across the three services.The Operation Sindoor testThe system's value was on view during Operation Sindoor, which began on May 7, 2025, with strikes on nine terrorist sites in Pakistan. IACCS coordinated both offensive and defensive operations, and a node was shown at the military briefing on May 12. It helped detect and track drones and missiles, including low-signature targets, and matched them with weapons such as the S-400, Akash and counter-drone systems, so that layers did not duplicate each other. Between May 8 and 10, Pakistani drones and missiles were intercepted. Akashteer had been tied in only months earlier.The upgrade builds on a Phase-III modernisation accelerated after Sindoor. For a force that expects drone swarms and saturation attacks in the next war, the speed at which a threat is spotted, ranked and answered will count as much as the weapons themselves.

articles.title: Could one daily pill narrow the diabetes treatment gap in the Global South?
articles.summary: Globally, one in nine people lives with diabetes, as blockbuster injectable drugs begin making way for tablets instead.
articles.body:
Medication that has been a lifeline for patients with uncontrollable diabetes is now slowly shifting from injections to pills, a move that could fundamentally alter treatment for the disease – and who can access it.

This shift could also affect the treatment of obesity, a long misunderstood condition once associated with overeating and laziness, rather than the metabolic disorder it is now recognised as.

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists therapy isn’t new. The first FDA-approved drug, Exenatide, hit the market in 2005 and was followed by Liraglutide in 2009, which was seen as a revolutionary alternative to insulin.

But the market has until recently been dominated by weekly injections like Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide), and Mounjaro (tirzepatide). These drugs have also proved successful for weight loss.

Now, once-daily oral GLP pills are emerging as an alternative, especially for the diabetes-stricken Global South.

Oral once-daily pills of the same wonder drug could make access more affordable, and less reliant on the cold chain that GLP-1 injections and insulin depend on – and that are harder to secure in emerging economies.

One in nine people in the world between the ages of 20-79 lives with diabetes, and one in eight people globally is obese.

The GLP injections come with a high price tag and are often not covered by insurance companies, which treat them as an elective drug.

In the United States, Eli Lily’s Mounjaro costs about $500 for a month’s worth of doses; in the UK, about 199 pounds ($264); and in Saudi Arabia, 1,261 riyals ($336). In India, the brand is locally manufactured and available at 14,766 rupees ($157). In Pakistan, the imported Mounjaro is a whopping 220,000 rupees ($723), while the locally manufactured Tirzepatide from Getz Pharma costs 17,000 rupees ($61).

While pills are usually taken once a day, injections are once per week.

Pakistan has the highest diabetes prevalence in the world – 31.4 percent of its population suffer from the disease – followed by the Marshall Islands (25.7 percent) and Kuwait (25.6 percent).

Many other Middle Eastern countries rank among nations with the highest diabetes prevalence.

For many countries in the Global South, the relative affordability of oral GLP drugs, where the locally manufactured oral semaglutide is about $18 for a 30-day supply, could make them more accessible for diabetes and obesity patients, remove the need for refrigeration and make rural distribution easier.

Dr Zakir Alavi is an endocrinologist in Karachi, Pakistan and has been treating patients with diabetes and obesity for nearly 30 years.

“Pakistan is a country of contrast. We have, on one hand, childhood malnutrition, underweight, and stunted growth. On the other hand, we have childhood and adult obesity,” said Alavi. “And surprisingly, there is at least some element in the adult and childhood obesity which can be linked to a malnourished mother, and an underweight, premature baby.”

Malnutrition during pregnancy can lead to low birth weight, and babies born small who gain weight rapidly in infancy face a higher risk of childhood obesity, according to doctors.

Alavi said GLP drugs – whether the injectables or pills – have revolutionised the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. They not only help type 2 diabetes patients manage their weight, but can also help non-diabetics tackle obesity, improving cardiac and renal outcomes, liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea and osteoarthritis.

“They can be used for management of all these things when weight reduction is important, or sugar control is important, or both,” he said.

Rayaz Malik is a professor of medicine at Weill Cornell Medica College Qatar, and a senior consultant at Hamad Medical Corporation in Doha. Malik has been at the front line of helping patients with diabetes and obesity, and he echoed Alavi’s views.

“We looked at how much weight you need to lose to cure diabetes, the magic number seemed to come in at around 15kg, at least,” he said, speaking of research on the subject.

With the wider availability of GLP medication in oral pill form, a cure for diabetes is closer than ever for many more people.

Jens Juul Holst is one of the central scientists behind the GLP revolution that has given millions around the world a way to live with diabetes and, for those struggling with obesity, a chance to reclaim their bodies.

A professor, physician and physiologist, Holst lives in Copenhagen and began his journey with gut hormones in the 1970s.

“When we discovered this, what we found was an insulin-releasing peptide from the gut,” Holst told Al Jazeera. “We were interested in what regulates insulin secretion, and that was as a physiological mechanism because we had some people who were developing too low blood glucose levels, [which is called] hypoglycemia, and we were looking for a peptide that could create insulin release stimulation and then be responsible for the low glucose levels.”

He says reactive hypoglycemia, which patients experience after certain operations like bariatric surgery, explains how the GLP molecule works.

Eventually, his team discovered that the molecule plays a role not only in insulin release and secretion, but also helps regulate appetite and food intake.

“The discovery of that was actually perhaps even more exciting than the discovery of its insulin-releasing activities,” Holst said, the excitement in his voice rising. “And then, the big day really was when we were able to infuse people with diabetes with this new peptide and see what happened.”

They found that an intravenous infusion of GLP-1 “would normalise blood glucose levels completely in people with long-standing, problematic type 2 diabetes and this happened in the course of four hours,” he said. “From then on, we knew that we were really onto something big.”

Holst and his team’s discovery led to what is now known as semaglutide, which paved the way for another drug, tirzepatide, and a third drug called retatrutide that is currently undergoing trials with a potential release in 2027.

Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two of the primary manufacturers, expect the GLP market to jump from $80bn per year to $135bn by 2030.

Obesity alone was responsible for 3.7 million deaths worldwide in 2024.

In December 2025, the World Health Organization issued guidelines recommending GLP-1 medicines as a long-term treatment for obesity, which affects more than 1 billion people globally.

“As we realised that it was a very good anti-diabetic therapy, it was obvious that millions could benefit from this,” Holst said.

“Because now you have a population which is 40 percent of the globe who would be interested in regulating body weight and the amount of interest would be huge,” he said, referring to the WHO’s 2016 estimate that 39 percent of adults worldwide are overweight. In 2024, WHO revised this estimate to 45 percent.

Injectable GLP medicines, particularly tirzepatide and semaglutide, remain the most effective treatments because they provide the strongest evidence for long-term weight loss and cardiovascular benefits.

The human gut releases a hormone called GLP-1 when we eat. As blood sugar rises, GLP-1 instructs your pancreas to release insulin. GIP is a gut hormone also released when we eat. Like GLP-1, it tells the pancreas to release insulin as blood sugar rises.

GLP-1 also slows how quickly food leaves your stomach, helping you feel full. GLP-1 medicines, therefore, mimic the hormone’s effects to lower blood sugar and reduce appetite.

Imagine a six-way traffic light when the lights aren’t working, leading to chaos over who can pass the intersection and who can’t.

Semaglutide, a GLP-1 drug, works on one receptor. This is like having a single-lane underpass at this intersection, meaning there is a guaranteed flow of traffic, albeit limited.

Tirzepatide is a GLP and a GIP, meaning it works on two receptors. That’s like having a signal-free overhead bridge, traffic lights at the intersection and an underpass making traffic much smoother. In effect, the organs and cells are rerouted to work the way they are supposed to.

Will oral GLP drugs work as well as the injections?

Oral GLP-1 medicines promise the convenience of a pill without sacrificing much of the weight-loss effect, but they still face one major hurdle: the stomach.

Unlike injections, which deliver the drug directly into the body, oral semaglutide must survive digestion before a small fraction is absorbed.

That is why it must be taken on an empty stomach and at a higher dose.

Newer oral GLP-1 drugs such as orforglipron, however, are designed to overcome those limits and can be taken without fasting.

While oral drugs appear capable of delivering similar results for many patients, there are still few head-to-head trials comparing pills directly with injections, experts say.

The biggest winners may be people in countries already carrying the world’s heaviest diabetes burden.

If future versions become available as tablets and prices fall after patent expiry, the impact in South Asia and the Middle East could be enormous.

Malik said once-a-week GLP oral medication isn’t that far from being a reality.

Meanwhile, he added, efforts are also under way to develop formulations of the current drugs that are much longer-acting – once-a-month doses might work.

What makes the GLP-1 drugs work is their ability to mimic what the body naturally does, Malik said.

“The clever way for treatment is to do what your human body is doing,” he said. “And it’s transforming people’s lives.”
